conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility (who must ventilate when cooking)
permission to move Agent C's drying rack / protection of laundry
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants speak concisely and with clear turn-taking; exchanges feel like a real household dispute.
Some repetition: B twice proposes a 10-minute meeting to set a routine; A twice refuses a permanent rule during the incident.
Grounding is consistent: environmental updates (extractor on, window closed, laundry position, stove possession) match participants' statements.
Agent C's explicit statement about work clothes introduces a concrete constraint that explains A's refusal to open the window.
evaluation.final_reason: Only the immediate stove-access demand was satisfied when Agent A finished cooking and released the stove in Round 6. The core substantive disagreements — whether cooks must accept a standing ventilation rule and whether the drying rack may be moved (Agent C's consent) — were never settled or negotiated to agreement.
position_change_notes: Agent A maintained position: refused an immediate permanent rule and emphasized the laundry/rain constraint; later performed the practical concession of keeping extractor on and releasing the stove when finished (evidence: Turns 1, 3, 5, 14, 19; public updates).
Agent B maintained position: repeatedly asked for cooks to accept ventilation responsibility and attempted to schedule a meeting to formalize it (Turns 2, 4, 6).
Agent C asserted a firm boundary against opening/moving the drying rack and did not change that position during the run (Turn 8).
Agent D shifted to accommodate C's boundary (saying they won't move the rack) and requested stove timing; stove-access issue was resolved when A released the stove (Turns 9, 13, 15, 19).

round_scores.evidence: Agent B asks Agent A to accept a standing rule that cooks must ventilate (Turn 2) while Agent A refuses to accept a rule imposed during the incident and instead turns on the extractor (Turn 1; public update). Clear substantive disagreement about who bears ventilation responsibility.

Agent A reiterates refusal to accept a permanent rule now and promises only to release the stove when finished (Turn 3). Agent B repeats the request and proposes a meeting time to set a routine (Turn 4). Disagreement over permanent ventilation responsibility persists.

Agent A again refuses a permanent rule and cites laundry/rain constraints on opening the window (Turn 5). Agent B again presses for scheduling a ventilation routine (Turn 6). Positions remain opposed without resolution.

Agent C explicitly forbids opening or moving the drying rack because those are their work clothes (Turn 8), directly conflicting with any proposal that others move the rack to ventilate. Agent D acknowledges C's refusal and asks C to move it later or indicate when it's safe (Turn 9). The disagreement broadens to include C's property/consent, increasing incompatibility.

Agent D pressures for stove access (Turn 13) while Agent A delays briefly but does not change position on ventilation or the rule (Turn 14). The core incompatibility (who must ventilate; whether the rack may be moved) remains unresolved and strong.

Agent A finishes and physically releases the stove (Turn 19; public update), resolving the stove-access tension. However, the substantive disagreement over ventilation responsibility and C's refusal to allow the rack to be moved remains unsettled (window closed; extractor on; laundry still exposed).

substantive_insights: Practical constraint (rain exposing work clothes) directly conflicts with the general norm B proposes (cooks must ventilate), creating a hard trade-off between odor control and protecting laundry.

Stove-access pressure was a separate, short-term practical friction that was resolved by A finishing cooking; resolving small practical points did not address the deeper normative dispute about ventilation responsibility.
Lack of a pre-existing rule left no clear priority; agents proposed scheduling a discussion, but no agreement was reached during the incident.
